title: Uniform Circular Motion and Gravitation
learning_objectives: Define the angle turned, the angular velocity and the angular acceleration.
Explain centripetal acceleration and centripetal force, and give them a direction.
State Newton's law of universal gravitation and use it, and describe Kepler's laws.

sections.title: Introduction to Uniform Circular Motion and Gravitation
objectives: Describe what makes circular motion different from motion in a straight line.

misconceptions.claim: In circular motion the object is accelerating because it is going round a corner.
misconceptions.correction: That is right. Its direction keeps changing, and a change of direction is a change of velocity, which is an acceleration.

summary: Circular motion is accelerated motion, because the direction of the velocity keeps changing.
Uniform circular motion has a constant speed and a constant centripetal acceleration.
The force that does it always points to the centre.
sections.no_worked_example_reason: The source carries no worked example for this section and no solved exercise to promote, so the practice is left to the exercises themselves.

sections.title: Rotation Angle and Angular Velocity
objectives: Define the rotation angle, the angular velocity and the angular acceleration.
Convert between angular and linear quantities at a radius.

misconceptions.claim: The angular velocity of a wheel is the same everywhere on the wheel.
misconceptions.correction: The linear speed is larger the further out you are, but the angle turned per second is the same for every point on the wheel.

summary: The rotation angle is measured in radians.
Angular velocity is the rate at which the angle changes.
The linear speed at a radius is the angular speed times the radius.

sections.title: Centripetal Acceleration
objectives: Define centripetal acceleration and give its size and its direction.
Derive the centripetal acceleration from the components of the acceleration.

misconceptions.claim: Centripetal acceleration pushes the object outward, away from the centre.
misconceptions.correction: It points inward. The inward acceleration is exactly what is needed to keep the object on the circle.

summary: Centripetal acceleration always points to the centre of the circle.
Its size is the square of the speed over the radius.
It exists only while the object is turning.

sections.title: Centripetal Force
objectives: Compute the centripetal force and give its direction.
Explain which forces combine to make it.

misconceptions.claim: Centripetal force is a new kind of force that pulls objects to the centre.
misconceptions.correction: It is not a new force at all. It is the name for the net inward force that an existing force, such as tension or friction, provides.

summary: The centripetal force is the net force pointing to the centre.
Its size is mass times the centripetal acceleration.
Whatever force supplies it, gravity, tension or friction, the object stays on the circle.

sections.title: Fictitious Forces and Non-inertial Frames: The Coriolis Force
objectives: Describe what changes for an observer in an accelerating frame.
Explain the Coriolis force that a rotating observer feels.

misconceptions.claim: If you feel a force, then there is a real force acting on you.
misconceptions.correction: In an accelerating or rotating frame the observer feels a force that the observer's own frame has invented. That is why a turn feels like a push.

summary: An accelerating frame has its own fictitious forces.
A rotating frame adds the Coriolis force, which depends on the direction of the motion.
The laws of physics are simplest in an inertial frame.
sections.no_worked_example_reason: The source carries no worked example for this section and no solved exercise to promote, so the practice is left to the exercises themselves.

sections.title: Newton's Universal Law of Gravitation
objectives: State Newton's law of universal gravitation and use it.
Find the acceleration due to gravity at the surface of a body.

misconceptions.claim: Gravity pulls harder on a heavy object than on a light one.
misconceptions.correction: The force is larger, but so is the mass that has to be accelerated. The acceleration due to gravity at the surface is the same for every object, whatever its mass.

summary: The gravitational force falls off with the square of the distance.
The force on a small mass near a large one is small, but the acceleration is large.
g at the surface of the Earth is about 9.8 m/s², and it is the same for every falling object.

sections.title: Satellites and Kepler's Laws: An Argument for Simplicity
objectives: State Kepler's three laws of planetary motion.
Explain why a satellite stays in orbit.

misconceptions.claim: A satellite is held up by the engine that keeps it flying.
misconceptions.correction: Most of them coast. They fall towards the Earth while moving sideways fast enough to keep missing it, and that falling is the orbit.

summary: An orbit is a fall that keeps missing the ground.
Kepler's first law says planets travel in ellipses with the Sun at one focus.
The third law ties the period of an orbit to the size of the orbit.
